This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

**Mistral** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)").[[1]](#cite_note-1) Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 1976. Mistral is named for the Chilean poet [Gabriela Mistral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriela_Mistral "Gabriela Mistral"), who lived from 1889 to 1957.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

A large irregular depression and several smaller ones are present in the southeastern part of the crater floor. A similar depression is present in the crater [Veronese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veronese_(crater) "Veronese (crater)") which overlies the northwest rim of Mistral, and small ones are present in the unnamed crater to the southwest. The depressions are similar to those within [Navoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navoi_(crater) "Navoi (crater)"), [Lermontov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lermontov_(crater) "Lermontov (crater)"), [Scarlatti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarlatti_(crater) "Scarlatti (crater)"), and [Praxiteles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praxiteles_(crater) "Praxiteles (crater)"). The depressions are thought to be caused by volcanic explosions.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

**Carducci** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). It has a diameter of 108.19 kilometers.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 1976. Carducci is named for the Italian poet [Giosuè Carducci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giosuè_Carducci "Giosuè Carducci"), who lived from 1835 to 1907.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

An unnamed crater of about 20 km (12 mi) diameter has obliterated the western portion of Carducci's central peak complex.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

**Hauptmann** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). It has a diameter of 118 kilometers.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 1985. Hauptmann is named for the German playwright [Gerhart Hauptmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhart_Hauptmann "Gerhart Hauptmann"), who lived from 1862 to 1946.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

There is an irregular depression next to the central peak complex of Hauptmann, making it a pit-floor crater. The depression may be caused by explosive volcanism.[[3]](#cite_note-Gillis-Davis2009-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Hauptmann is south of [Kālidāsā](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kālidāsā_(crater) "Kālidāsā (crater)") crater and northwest of [Milton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_(crater) "Milton (crater)"). A dark spot of low reflectance material (LRM) is present to the southwest of Hauptmann.

**Kipling** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). It has a diameter of 164 kilometers. Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 2010. Kipling is named for the British author [Rudyard Kipling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudyard_Kipling "Rudyard Kipling"), who lived from 1865 to 1936.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

There is a large, irregular depression within Kipling that is probably a volcanic pit. It was likely caused by multiple eruptions and it is called a compound vent.[[2]](#cite_note-2) The pit is also a confirmed *dark spot*.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Kipling is north of the smaller [Capote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capote_(crater) "Capote (crater)") crater. To the northwest of Kipling is the small but prominent crater [David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_(crater) "David (crater)"), which is also a *dark spot*.

**Laxness** is a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), located near the north pole. It was named by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 2013, after [Icelandic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland "Iceland") writer [Halldór Laxness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halldór_Laxness "Halldór Laxness").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

[S band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S_band "S band") radar data from the [Arecibo Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arecibo_Observatory "Arecibo Observatory") collected between 1999 and 2005 indicates a radar-bright area along the southern interior of Laxness, which is probably indicative of a water ice deposit, and lies within the permanently shadowed part of the crater.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

[Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuller_(crater) "Fuller (crater)") crater is southeast of Laxness. Both lie in the northern part of the [Goethe Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goethe_Basin "Goethe Basin").

# Yeats (crater)

**Yeats** is an [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on the planet [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). It is named after [William Butler Yeats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Butler_Yeats "William Butler Yeats"), an [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") poet and dramatist. The name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1976.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)

![}](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Yeats_crater_EN0131772058M.jpg/330px-Yeats_crater_EN0131772058M.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

The rim of Yeats is circular and intact, except where an indentation is made by a crater on the north side. It is bordered by a smaller, unnamed crater to the northwest. There is a scarp cutting across the crater which trends northeast. The central peak is complex, and there are [hollows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollows_(Mercury) "Hollows (Mercury)") on the east and west sides of the peak.

Yeats is located south of the crater [Li Po](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Po_(crater) "Li Po (crater)") and southwest of the crater [Sinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinan_(crater) "Sinan (crater)").
